title: Agent Skills
description: Packaging repeatable instructions as a SKILL.md file Claude discovers and invokes on its own.
content:
## What it is

A **skill** is a directory containing a `SKILL.md` file: YAML frontmatter that tells Claude when
to use it, followed by markdown instructions for what to do. That's the whole mechanism — no
special runtime, no registration step beyond putting the file in the right place.

The point is the same one behind extracting a shell function instead of retyping a command: if
you keep pasting the same checklist, the same multi-step procedure, or the same "when you see X,
do Y" into chat, that's a skill. It's also the fix for a `CLAUDE.md` that has grown past facts
into procedure — `CLAUDE.md` content is always in context; a skill's body loads only when it's
actually invoked, so long reference material costs nothing until you need it.

Claude Code skills follow the open [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) standard, so a skill
written for Claude Code is (mostly) portable to other tools that implement the same spec. Claude
Code layers a few of its own extensions on top — invocation control, running a skill in an
isolated subagent, and injecting live shell output into the prompt — covered below.

## How to use it

### Write one

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/summarize-changes
```

```yaml title="~/.claude/skills/summarize-changes/SKILL.md"
---
description: Summarizes uncommitted changes and flags anything risky. Use when the user asks what changed, wants a commit message, or asks to review their diff.
---

## Current changes

!`git diff HEAD`

## Instructions

Summarize the changes above in two or three bullet points, then list any risks — missing error
handling, hardcoded values, tests that need updating. If the diff is empty, say so.
```

The `` !`git diff HEAD` `` line is **dynamic context injection**: Claude Code runs that shell
command before the skill content reaches Claude and splices in the real output, so the
instructions arrive already grounded in your actual working tree. This only runs inside Claude
Code, not in the portable subset of the spec.

Either ask about your changes in plain language (Claude loads the skill automatically because
the request matches `description`), or invoke it directly:

```text
/summarize-changes
```

### Discovery flow

Only the `description` (plus `when_to_use`, if set) sits in context all the time — that's how
Claude decides *whether* a skill applies without paying for its full body on every turn. The
full markdown loads only once the skill actually fires, and then it stays loaded for the rest of
the session; re-invoking the identical skill doesn't duplicate it.

### Where skills live

| Location | Path | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Personal | `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | All your projects |
| Project | `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | This repo, shareable via git |
| Plugin | `<plugin>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | Wherever the plugin is enabled |
| Enterprise | Managed settings | Every user in the org |

Project skills are discovered walking up from your working directory to the repo root, and
nested `.claude/skills/` directories (e.g. inside a monorepo package) load the moment Claude
touches a file in that subtree. When names collide, enterprise beats personal beats project, and
any of those beats a bundled skill with the same name.

Only `SKILL.md` is required. Everything else — reference docs, templates, scripts — is optional
weight that Claude reads or executes only when the skill's own instructions point to it. This is
the same "keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines, push detail into linked files" discipline that keeps
the always-resident `description` cheap.

### Frontmatter fields

Every field is optional; only `description` is genuinely recommended, since it's what drives
automatic discovery.

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `name` | Display name in listings. The directory name is still what you type to invoke it, for personal/project skills. |
| `description` | What the skill does and when to use it — this is what Claude matches against your prompt. |
| `disable-model-invocation` | `true` means only you can trigger it (`/name`), never Claude on its own. Use for anything with side effects: deploys, commits, sending a Slack message. |
| `user-invocable` | `false` hides it from the `/` menu — background knowledge Claude should know about but that isn't a meaningful command for you to run by hand. |
| `allowed-tools` | Tools pre-approved without a permission prompt for the turn that invokes this skill. Clears on your next message. |
| `disallowed-tools` | Tools removed from the pool while the skill is active. |
| `argument-hint` | Autocomplete hint, e.g. `[issue-number]`. |
| `model`, `effort` | Override just for the turn this skill runs. |
| `context: fork` | Run the skill's instructions in an isolated subagent instead of inline — see [Subagents](/docs/subagents). |
| `paths` | Glob patterns; the skill only auto-loads when Claude is working with matching files. |

`$ARGUMENTS` (or `$0`, `$1`, …, or named via an `arguments` list) substitutes whatever follows
the skill name when invoked, e.g. `/fix-issue 123` making `$ARGUMENTS` expand to `123`.

### Skills vs. slash commands, subagents, and MCP

These four get confused because they overlap in what they enable, not in what they *are*:

| | What it actually is | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|
| **Skill** | A markdown file with instructions, loaded into the *current* context | You keep re-explaining the same procedure or convention |
| **Slash command** | Now unified with skills — a skill is what a custom command creates | (same as above; legacy `.claude/commands/*.md` still works) |
| **Subagent** | A *separate* context window with its own system prompt and tool access | The work would flood your main conversation with output you won't need again |
| **MCP server** | An external process exposing tools/resources over a protocol | You need to talk to a real system — a database, an API, a ticketing tool |

A skill can *use* a subagent (`context: fork`) for isolation, and a subagent can *preload* skills
as reference material via its `skills:` frontmatter field — they compose rather than compete.
None of them replace MCP: a skill can tell Claude how to use an MCP tool well, but it can't call
an external system by itself without one.

## Best practices

* **Front-load the trigger in `description`.** Claude matches your prompt against this field
  alone before ever reading the body — a vague description means the skill never fires
  automatically.
* **`disable-model-invocation: true` on anything with side effects.** You don't want Claude
  deciding to deploy because the code looks ready. Reserve automatic invocation for skills that
  are safe to trigger on a guess.
* **Keep `SKILL.md` short; push detail into linked files.** The body persists in context for the
  rest of the session once loaded — every line is a recurring cost, not a one-time read.
* **Write standing instructions, not one-time steps.** Claude Code doesn't re-read the file on
  later turns; if guidance should hold for the whole task, phrase it that way.
* **Scope `allowed-tools` narrowly and to real commands**, e.g.
  `Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *)`, not a blanket `Bash` grant — this is exactly the kind of
  self-granted access you should be suspicious of when reviewing someone *else's* skill, which is
  the subject of the next page.

## A real example

A project skill that runs a project's lint suite and reports only failures — useful because the
full lint output can be hundreds of lines you don't want cluttering the main conversation:

```yaml title=".claude/skills/lint-check/SKILL.md"
---
name: lint-check
description: Runs the project's linter and reports only the failures. Use before committing or when asked to check code quality.
allowed-tools: Bash(golangci-lint run *)
context: fork
---

Run `golangci-lint run ./...` and report only the failing lint rules, grouped by file. If
everything passes, say so in one line — don't restate the command output.
```

Because `context: fork` is set, this runs in its own subagent: the (potentially huge) raw
linter output never touches the main conversation's context, and only the summary comes back.

title: Agent Teams
description: Coordinating multiple Claude Code sessions on one task, and when the coordination overhead is worth it.
content:
## What it is

Most Claude Code usage is one session, one context window. [Subagents](/docs/subagents) extend
that from inside the session — the main agent delegates a side task to a helper that reports back
a summary and disappears. This page is about the next level up: **running several independent
Claude Code sessions on the same piece of work, at the same time**, and having them coordinate.

There are two ways this actually happens, and it's worth keeping them distinct:

1. **Agent teams** — an experimental, named Claude Code feature. One session (the **lead**)
   spawns other full Claude Code sessions (**teammates**), each with its own context window. They
   share a task list, claim work, and message each other directly — the lead doesn't have to
   relay everything.
2. **Manual parallel sessions** — no special feature at all, just you opening several terminals
   (or [tmux](/docs/tmux) panes) and running `claude` in each, typically one per
   [git worktree](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree) so the sessions don't collide on files.
   Claude Code supports this directly with `claude --worktree <name>`.

Both are "agent teams" in the loose, workflow sense of the phrase. Only the first is a specific
product feature with that name, and it's still experimental — behind a flag, subject to change,
with documented rough edges around session resumption and shutdown. The rest of this page covers
both, and says clearly which is which.

## How subagents and agent teams differ

| | Subagents | Agent teams |
|---|---|---|
| **Process** | Runs inside the caller's session | Separate Claude Code session per teammate |
| **Context** | Own context window, returns a summary to the caller | Own context window, fully independent |
| **Communication** | Reports back to the main agent only | Teammates message each other directly |
| **Coordination** | Main agent manages all delegation | Shared task list; teammates self-claim work |
| **Token cost** | Lower — most work is summarized away | Higher — every teammate is a full Claude instance |
| **Best for** | A focused side task where only the result matters | Work that benefits from discussion or independent parallel exploration |

## How to use it

### The built-in feature

Agent teams ship behind an experimental flag. Enable it in `settings.json`:

```json title="~/.claude/settings.json"
{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS": "1"
  }
}
```

With it enabled, ask for a team in plain language and Claude spawns and coordinates it:

```text
Spawn three teammates to review this PR:
- one focused on security implications
- one checking performance impact
- one validating test coverage
Have them each review and report findings.
```

Claude decides how many teammates a task needs unless you say so explicitly. The lead's terminal
shows a panel listing teammates below the prompt; arrow keys select one, Enter opens its
transcript so you can read or message it directly, Escape interrupts its current turn.

Under the hood, the team is built from three pieces:

* **Task list** — pending / in-progress / completed work items, some with dependencies on others.
  Teammates self-claim the next unblocked task when they finish one, or the lead assigns work
  explicitly.
* **Mailbox** — each teammate has an inbox; `SendMessage`-style delivery is automatic, so the lead
  doesn't need to poll for updates. When a teammate goes idle, it notifies the lead.
* **Display mode** — teammates run **in-process** by default (all inside your one terminal,
  switched between via the agent panel) or in **split panes**, one pane per teammate, which
  requires [tmux](/docs/tmux) or iTerm2. See
  [Agent Teams with tmux](/docs/agent-teams-tmux) for that setup in full.

Two other controls worth knowing:

* **Plan approval** — for risky work, ask a teammate to plan before touching files: *"Spawn an
  architect teammate to refactor the auth module. Require plan approval before making changes."*
  It works in read-only plan mode until the lead approves.
* **Reusable roles** — a teammate can be spawned from a named [subagent](/docs/subagents)
  definition (project, user, or plugin-scoped), so a `security-reviewer` role works both as an
  on-demand subagent and as a team role, defined once.

### The manual pattern

You don't need the experimental flag to run multiple Claude Code sessions on one task — this is
just running `claude` more than once, deliberately kept isolated:

```bash
claude --worktree feature-auth      # terminal 1: isolated checkout on its own branch
claude --worktree fix-rate-limit    # terminal 2: a second isolated checkout
```

Each `--worktree` invocation creates a real `git worktree` — a separate working directory on its
own branch, checked out from the same repository — so two sessions editing "the same project" are
never editing the same files on disk. This is the mechanism [Agent Teams with
tmux](/docs/agent-teams-tmux) builds a concrete layout around: one pane per session, one worktree
per pane.

The manual pattern gives up the shared task list and inter-agent messaging the built-in feature
provides — you are the coordination layer, reading each session's output and deciding what
happens next. In exchange, it needs no flag, has no experimental-feature caveats, and is exactly
as debuggable as running Claude Code normally, because that's all it is.

## When it's worth the complexity

Both forms of "multiple agents" cost more than one session: more tokens (every teammate is a full
context window), more attention (someone has to read what each one produces), and — for the
built-in feature specifically — you're opting into an experimental code path.

They're worth it when:

* **The work is genuinely parallel and independent.** Three people could do these three things at
  the same time without talking to each other much. New modules, a security/performance/test
  three-way review, cross-layer changes (frontend, backend, tests) each owned by one worker.
* **Competing hypotheses beat one investigation.** A single agent (like a single engineer)
  anchors on the first plausible theory it finds. Several agents independently investigating a bug
  and actively trying to disprove each other converge on the real root cause faster than one
  agent going down one path.
* **You want review from different angles on the same artifact.** One reviewer tends to focus on
  one category of issue at a time; three reviewers with three different mandates catch more, in
  parallel, than one reviewer catching three things in sequence.

They're not worth it — plain subagents or a single session serve better — when:

* **The work is sequential or has heavy dependencies.** If step 2 needs step 1's output, teammates
  spend most of their time waiting or re-coordinating, and you've paid for parallelism you can't
  use.
* **Multiple workers would touch the same files.** Two agents editing one file is a conflict
  generator, not a speedup — this applies whether it's two subagents, two teammates, or two people.
* **It's routine work a single session handles fine.** Coordination overhead (spawning, task
  handoffs, synthesizing results) isn't free even when it doesn't cause conflicts. Reach for teams
  when the parallel exploration is the point, not by default.

## Best practices

* **Start with research and review, not implementation**, if you're new to this. Reviewing a PR
  from three angles has clear task boundaries and low conflict risk; parallel code-writing has
  both.
* **Give each teammate real context in the spawn prompt.** Teammates load `CLAUDE.md`, skills, and
  MCP servers automatically, but not the lead's conversation history — say what you'd tell a new
  hire walking into the task cold.
* **Size the team to the task, not the ceiling.** Three to five teammates is a reasonable range for
  most work; more teammates adds coordination overhead and token cost without proportional speedup.
* **One owner per file.** Whether it's the built-in feature or manual worktrees, decide up front
  who owns which files or modules so nobody's overwriting anybody else's edits.
* **Stay in the loop.** Check in on progress, redirect approaches that have gone sideways, and
  synthesize findings as they arrive rather than walking away for an hour. An unattended team
  running the wrong direction for a long time is expensive in a way an unattended single session
  usually isn't.
* **Prefer subagents when workers don't need to talk to each other.** If the only communication
  path you need is "worker reports back to me," that's the cheaper, simpler tool — see
  [Subagents](/docs/subagents).

With it enabled, ask for a team in plain language and Claude spawns and coordinates it:

text
Spawn three teammates to review this PR:
- one focused on security implications
- one checking performance impact
- one validating test coverage
Have them each review and report findings.

Claude decides how many teammates a task needs unless you say so explicitly. The lead's terminal
shows a panel listing teammates below the prompt; arrow keys select one, Enter opens its
transcript so you can read or message it directly, Escape interrupts its current turn.

Under the hood, the team is built from three pieces:

* **Task list** — pending / in-progress / completed work items, some with dependencies on others.
  Teammates self-claim the next unblocked task when they finish one, or the lead assigns work
  explicitly.
* **Mailbox** — each teammate has an inbox;

-style delivery is automatic, so the lead
  doesn't need to poll for updates. When a teammate goes idle, it notifies the lead.
* **Display mode** — teammates run **in-process** by default (all inside your one terminal,
  switched between via the agent panel) or in **split panes**, one pane per teammate, which
  requires [tmux](/docs/tmux) or iTerm2. See
  [Agent Teams with tmux](/docs/agent-teams-tmux) for that setup in full.

Two other controls worth knowing:

* **Plan approval** — for risky work, ask a teammate to plan before touching files: *"Spawn an
  architect teammate to refactor the auth module. Require plan approval before making changes."*
  It works in read-only plan mode until the lead approves.
* **Reusable roles** — a teammate can be spawned from a named [subagent](/docs/subagents)
  definition (project, user, or plugin-scoped), so a

role works both as an
  on-demand subagent and as a team role, defined once.

### The manual pattern

You don't need the experimental flag to run multiple Claude Code sessions on one task — this is
just running
more than once, deliberately kept isolated:

bash
claude --worktree feature-auth      # terminal 1: isolated checkout on its own branch
claude --worktree fix-rate-limit    # terminal 2: a second isolated checkout

— a separate working directory on its
own branch, checked out from the same repository — so two sessions editing "the same project" are
never editing the same files on disk. This is the mechanism [Agent Teams with
tmux](/docs/agent-teams-tmux) builds a concrete layout around: one pane per session, one worktree
per pane.

The manual pattern gives up the shared task list and inter-agent messaging the built-in feature
provides — you are the coordination layer, reading each session's output and deciding what
happens next. In exchange, it needs no flag, has no experimental-feature caveats, and is exactly
as debuggable as running Claude Code normally, because that's all it is.

## When it's worth the complexity

Both forms of "multiple agents" cost more than one session: more tokens (every teammate is a full
context window), more attention (someone has to read what each one produces), and — for the
built-in feature specifically — you're opting into an experimental code path.

They're worth it when:

* **The work is genuinely parallel and independent.** Three people could do these three things at
  the same time without talking to each other much. New modules, a security/performance/test
  three-way review, cross-layer changes (frontend, backend, tests) each owned by one worker.
* **Competing hypotheses beat one investigation.** A single agent (like a single engineer)
  anchors on the first plausible theory it finds. Several agents independently investigating a bug
  and actively trying to disprove each other converge on the real root cause faster than one
  agent going down one path.
* **You want review from different angles on the same artifact.** One reviewer tends to focus on
  one category of issue at a time; three reviewers with three different mandates catch more, in
  parallel, than one reviewer catching three things in sequence.

They're not worth it — plain subagents or a single session serve better — when:

* **The work is sequential or has heavy dependencies.** If step 2 needs step 1's output, teammates
  spend most of their time waiting or re-coordinating, and you've paid for parallelism you can't
  use.
* **Multiple workers would touch the same files.** Two agents editing one file is a conflict
  generator, not a speedup — this applies whether it's two subagents, two teammates, or two people.
* **It's routine work a single session handles fine.** Coordination overhead (spawning, task
  handoffs, synthesizing results) isn't free even when it doesn't cause conflicts. Reach for teams
  when the parallel exploration is the point, not by default.

## Best practices

* **Start with research and review, not implementation**, if you're new to this. Reviewing a PR
  from three angles has clear task boundaries and low conflict risk; parallel code-writing has
  both.
* **Give each teammate real context in the spawn prompt.** Teammates load

title: Agent Teams with tmux
description: A practical tmux layout for running several Claude Code agents side by side, each on its own git worktree.
content:
## What it is

[Agent Teams](/docs/agent-teams) covers *why* and *when* to run several Claude Code sessions on
one task, whether that's the experimental built-in team feature or manually opening multiple
`claude` sessions yourself. [tmux](/docs/tmux) covers the terminal multiplexer itself — sessions,
windows, panes, persistence.

This page is the join: **using tmux panes so you can watch and steer several Claude Code agents at
once, in one screen, without them stepping on each other's files.** This is a genuinely documented
integration point, not just a coincidence of two useful tools — Claude Code's built-in agent teams
feature has a **split-pane display mode that requires tmux** (or iTerm2) to show one teammate per
pane. The same layout is also exactly what you'd build by hand for the manual multi-session
pattern. Both paths land on the same picture.

## The core problem: agents and files

Run two Claude Code agents against the same working directory and they can edit the same file at
the same time. Nothing in either agent knows the other exists unless you've set up the built-in
team's shared task list — and even then, "don't touch the same file" is a convention the team has
to honor, not a lock the filesystem enforces.

The fix is the same one [Agent Teams](/docs/agent-teams) already names: **one git worktree per
agent.** A worktree is a separate checkout of the same repository, on its own branch, living in
its own directory — so two agents "working on the same project" are, on disk, working in two
completely separate directory trees that happen to share git history.

```bash
git worktree add ../myapp-auth feature-auth
git worktree add ../myapp-ratelimit fix-rate-limit
git worktree list
```

Claude Code's own `--worktree` flag does the `git worktree add` step for you and drops you
straight into a session inside it:

```bash
claude --worktree feature-auth
```

## A suggested tmux layout

One tmux window, one pane per agent, each pane's shell already `cd`'d into that agent's worktree
before Claude Code starts:

Building it by hand:

```bash
tmux new -s agents -n myapp          # session "agents", window "myapp"

# Pane 0 (created with the window) — first agent
cd ~/myapp-auth && claude --worktree feature-auth

# prefix %  → split right, second agent
cd ~/myapp-ratelimit && claude --worktree fix-rate-limit

# prefix "  → split the new pane down, third agent
cd ~/myapp-tests && claude --worktree add-tests
```

`prefix q` briefly shows pane numbers so you can jump straight to one; `prefix o` cycles focus;
`prefix z` zooms the pane you're reading into fullscreen and back when you want to focus on one
agent's output without losing the others. Full keybinding reference is on the [tmux
page](/docs/tmux).

## Naming conventions

Names are the only thing standing between you and a screen of identical-looking panes at 2am.
Two conventions worth committing to:

* **Session and window names match the repo and task**, not a date or a number:
  `tmux new -s agents -n myapp` reads back cleanly in `tmux ls`; `tmux new -s s1` does not.
* **Worktree directory names match the branch**, and pane titles (or just the shell prompt) should
  make it obvious which worktree you're in. `~/myapp-auth` on branch `feature-auth`, not
  `~/myapp2`. If you rename windows as you go (`prefix ,`), name each one after the branch the
  agent in it is working on — `feature-auth`, `fix-rate-limit` — so `prefix w`'s window picker is
  itself a status board.

## Avoiding agents stepping on each other

* **One worktree per agent, always.** This is the load-bearing rule; naming conventions are just
  bookkeeping on top of it. Two agents in one directory is the one setup that reliably produces
  conflicting edits.
* **Watch for shared resources outside the file tree.** Worktrees isolate files, not databases,
  ports, or external services. Two agents both trying to bind `:8080`, or both migrating the same
  dev database, will collide even with perfect worktree isolation — give each a distinct port or
  database name via env vars per pane if agents will run the app.
* **Merge deliberately, not automatically.** Worktrees on separate branches don't merge
  themselves. Decide the merge order up front, especially if two branches touch overlapping code
  even from different worktrees — the isolation prevents live-edit conflicts, not eventual merge
  conflicts.
* **Clean up worktrees you're done with**, the same way you'd clean up a stale session:
  ```bash
  git worktree remove ../myapp-auth
  git worktree prune
  ```

## Practical tips

* **Turn on tmux mouse mode** (`set -g mouse on`, see the [tmux starter
  config](/docs/tmux#a-starter-tmuxconf)) so clicking into a pane to read or redirect an agent
  doesn't require memorizing navigation keys first.
* **Detach, don't close.** `prefix d` leaves every agent running; closing the terminal window
  might too, depending on your terminal, but detaching is the version you control on purpose.
  Reattach later with `tmux attach -t agents` and every pane — and every agent — is exactly where
  you left it.
* **Check `tmux ls` for orphans.** If a Claude Code session that opened split panes itself doesn't
  get cleanly shut down, it's possible for the underlying tmux session to outlive it. List
  sessions and kill anything stale:
  ```bash
  tmux ls
  tmux kill-session -t <name>
  ```
* **Don't run more agents than you can actually read.** A four-pane layout you glance across
  regularly beats an eight-pane layout where half the agents drift unattended for twenty minutes.
  [Agent Teams](/docs/agent-teams#best-practices) makes the same point about team size for the
  same underlying reason — attention doesn't parallelize as well as the agents do.
* **Zoom in before making a decision.** `prefix z` on one pane before approving a plan or reading a
  long diff — a quarter-width pane is fine for glancing at progress, not for reviewing code.

## A real example

Three independent fixes landed in one PR review pass, run in parallel:

```bash
git worktree add ../billing-refund fix/refund-rounding
git worktree add ../billing-webhook fix/webhook-retry
git worktree add ../billing-tests test/coverage-gaps

tmux new -s billing -n fixes
cd ~/billing-refund  && claude --worktree fix/refund-rounding
```

`prefix %`, then in the new right-hand pane:

```bash
cd ~/billing-webhook && claude --worktree fix/webhook-retry
```

`prefix "` on that pane to split it downward, then:

```bash
cd ~/billing-tests   && claude --worktree test/coverage-gaps
```

Three agents, three branches, three panes, zero shared files. `prefix o` cycles through to check
progress; `prefix z` zooms whichever one needs a real look; `prefix d` detaches for lunch and
`tmux attach -t billing` picks the whole layout back up afterward — all three agents still
running, nothing lost. When each branch is ready, review and merge them in whatever order makes
sense, same as reviewing three separate engineers' PRs.

title: Memory - CLAUDE.md
description: How Claude Code loads persistent project and personal instructions.
content:
## What it is

Every Claude Code session starts with an empty context window — no memory of yesterday's session
carries over on its own. `CLAUDE.md` is how you give it persistent instructions anyway: a plain
markdown file, loaded fresh at the start of every session, that Claude treats as context rather
than enforced configuration. This repo's own `AGENTS.md` (imported by `CLAUDE.md` at the project
root) is exactly this mechanism in use — the rules about the sidebar not being automatic, the
`/docs` prefix on Card hrefs, and the section-shape conventions all live there because they're
things worth re-stating every session rather than re-discovering by trial and error.

Claude Code also has a second, separate memory system: **auto memory**, notes Claude writes to
itself in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/` based on corrections you give it during a
session. CLAUDE.md is what *you* write; auto memory is what *Claude* writes. Both load every
session; this page is about the one you control directly.

## How it loads

CLAUDE.md files exist at several scopes, loaded in this order — broadest to most specific, so
project instructions are the last (and therefore most emphasized) thing Claude reads:

| Scope | Location | Shared with |
|---|---|---|
| Managed policy | `/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md` (Linux), platform equivalent elsewhere | Everyone on the machine, enforced by IT |
| User | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` | Just you, across all projects |
| Project | `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` | The whole team, via git |
| Local | `./CLAUDE.local.md` | Just you, this project — gitignored |

Claude Code walks up the directory tree from your working directory, loading `CLAUDE.md` and
`CLAUDE.local.md` from every directory it passes through. Files at the repo root load in full at
launch; `CLAUDE.md` files in *subdirectories* load only when Claude actually reads a file in that
subdirectory — they aren't pulled into context just because they exist. Within one directory,
`CLAUDE.local.md` loads after `CLAUDE.md`, so your personal notes are the last thing read at that
level.

Run `/context` in a session to see exactly which memory files actually loaded — the fastest way
to confirm a file you just added is being picked up.

## Imports with `@path`

A CLAUDE.md can pull in other files with `@path/to/file`:

```markdown
See @README for project overview and @package.json for available npm commands.

# Additional Instructions
- git workflow: @docs/git-instructions.md
```

Imported files are expanded into context at launch, alongside the file that references them, and
can recursively import up to four hops deep. Wrapping a path in backticks (`` `@README` ``) keeps
it literal text instead of triggering an import — useful when you just want to *mention* a path.

This is exactly how this project's root `CLAUDE.md` works: it's a one-line `@AGENTS.md` import, so
the actual instructions live in a file other tools (or humans) can read directly, and Claude Code
just pulls it in. That pattern — `@AGENTS.md` plus Claude-specific additions below it — is the
recommended way to share one instructions file across multiple AI coding tools:

```markdown title="CLAUDE.md"
@AGENTS.md

## Claude Code

Use plan mode for changes under src/billing/.
```

## `/memory` and troubleshooting

`/memory` lists every CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md location across scopes — including ones that
don't exist yet — and opens the one you pick in your editor. If Claude isn't following an
instruction:

1. Run `/context` and check the **Memory files** list — if the file isn't there, Claude never saw
   it.
2. Check it's in a location that actually loads for this session (see the table above).
3. Make the instruction more specific. "Use 2-space indentation" is followed far more reliably
   than "format code nicely" — CLAUDE.md is context Claude tries to follow, not enforced
   configuration, so specificity is what compliance actually depends on.
4. Look for contradictions across files. Two CLAUDE.md files giving different guidance for the
   same thing means Claude picks one arbitrarily.

CLAUDE.md content also survives `/compact`: the project-root file is re-read from disk and

title: Code Organization
description: How to structure a Go project as it grows.
content:
## Layout is a late decision

The most common mistake with a new Go service is opening with a twelve-directory skeleton copied
from a blog post. You end up maintaining boundaries that don't correspond to anything real yet.

Go projects are unusually cheap to reorganize: packages are directories, imports are paths, and
`gopls` renames both for you. So the honest strategy is to **start small and split when a specific
pain appears**. This page is about recognizing that pain and knowing which split relieves it.

The mechanics of packages themselves — naming, `internal/`, `go mod` — are covered in
[Packages & Modules](/docs/golang-fundamentals/packages-modules). The *architectural* question of
which direction dependencies point is [Software Architecture Patterns](/docs/software-architecture-patterns).
This page is the practical middle: where the files actually go.

## The three shapes a service passes through

Almost every Go backend moves through these in order. Each move should be triggered by a problem,
not a calendar.

| Shape | Good until | The pain that ends it |
|---|---|---|
| One package | ~1,000 lines | You can't find anything, and everything can call everything |
| Packages by layer | ~10,000 lines | Adding one feature means editing four packages |
| Packages by domain | A long time | Two domains need to be separate services |

### Shape 1 — one package

For a small service, a handful of files in `main` is genuinely correct:

Everything is in one package, so there are no import decisions to make and no cycles possible.
Files are still a real organizing tool — `handler.go` and `store.go` separate concerns for a human
reader even when the compiler sees one package.

### Shape 2 — split by layer

The first split most services need. Each package holds one *kind* of thing:

This buys you an enforced rule: `repository` cannot import `handler`, so SQL can never leak
upward. That's real value, and for many services it's where the story ends.

Its limit shows up when you add a feature. "Add order cancellation" means touching
`handler/order.go`, `service/order.go`, and `repository/order_postgres.go` — three packages, one
concept. The code that changes together doesn't live together.

### Shape 3 — split by domain

Reorganize around what the code is *about* rather than what it *is*:

Now order cancellation is one directory. The package boundary also becomes meaningful: `user` can
expose a small API to `order` and hide the rest, which the layered shape can't do because
everything in `service` is one package.

## Naming

One rule with outsized impact: **name a package for what it provides, not what it contains.**
`payment`, `auth`, `ratelimit` — never `utils`, `common`, `helpers`, or `models`. A package named
for a category has no reason to reject any code, so it grows forever and everything imports it.
[Packages & Modules](/docs/golang-fundamentals/packages-modules) covers this and the
`internal/` rules in full.

## Breaking an import cycle

Go refuses to compile circular imports. This is a feature — it's the compiler telling you a
boundary is wrong — but the first time it happens it's genuinely confusing.

The classic version: `order` needs a user's email to send a confirmation, and `user` needs a
user's order count to decide their tier. Each imports the other, and the build fails:

The fix is not a third `shared` package — that just moves the problem and creates the grab-bag
you were warned about. Instead, **the consumer declares an interface for what it needs**, and the
provider satisfies it implicitly:

```go showLineNumbers title="internal/order/service.go"
package order

// order does NOT import user. It states its requirement locally.
type UserFinder interface {
    EmailFor(ctx context.Context, userID int64) (string, error)
}

type Service struct {
    users UserFinder
    store Store
}
```

```go showLineNumbers title="internal/user/service.go"
package user

// user knows nothing about order. It just has the method.
func (s *Service) EmailFor(ctx context.Context, userID int64) (string, error) {
    u, err := s.store.GetByID(ctx, userID)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return u.Email, nil
}
```

```go showLineNumbers title="cmd/api/main.go"
userSvc := user.NewService(userStore)
orderSvc := order.NewService(orderStore, userSvc)   // satisfies order.UserFinder
```

The arrow now runs one way, both packages compile alone, and `order` is testable with a
three-line fake. This is [Dependency Inversion](/docs/solid-principles) doing real work.

## The composition root

Every dependency in the program gets constructed in exactly one place: `main`. Nothing else
creates a database pool, reads an environment variable, or decides which implementation to use.

```go showLineNumbers title="cmd/api/main.go"
func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        slog.Error("startup failed", "err", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func run() error {
    ctx := context.Background()

    cfg, err := config.Load()
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("loading config: %w", err)
    }

    pool, err := db.New(ctx, cfg.DatabaseURL)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("connecting to database: %w", err)
    }
    defer pool.Close()

    // Wiring: adapters first, then the services that use them.
    userStore := postgres.NewUserStore(pool)
    orderStore := postgres.NewOrderStore(pool)

    userSvc := user.NewService(userStore)
    orderSvc := order.NewService(orderStore, userSvc)

    srv := &http.Server{
        Addr:    cfg.Addr,
        Handler: httpapi.NewRouter(userSvc, orderSvc),
    }
    return srv.ListenAndServe()
}
```

## Config

Load configuration once, in `main`, into a struct — never call `os.Getenv` deep inside a service.
A service that reads the environment can't be tested with different values and hides its
requirements from the reader.

```go showLineNumbers title="internal/config/config.go"
package config

type Config struct {
    Addr        string
    DatabaseURL string
    LogLevel    string
}

func Load() (Config, error) {
    cfg := Config{
        Addr:     envOr("ADDR", ":8080"),
        LogLevel: envOr("LOG_LEVEL", "info"),
    }

    cfg.DatabaseURL = os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL")
    if cfg.DatabaseURL == "" {
        return Config{}, errors.New("DATABASE_URL is required")
    }
    return cfg, nil
}

func envOr(key, fallback string) string {
    if v := os.Getenv(key); v != "" {
        return v
    }
    return fallback
}
```

Failing at startup on a missing required variable is correct — far better than a nil pointer
twenty minutes into production traffic.

## Where the non-Go files go

Two conventions the tooling actually knows about: `cmd/<name>/main.go` gives you one binary per
subdirectory, and **`testdata/` is ignored by the Go tool** — it's the standard home for fixtures
and golden files, covered in [Testing](/docs/testing).

## A real example

A mature layout, with the reason for each boundary rather than a rule:

* **`internal/order` and `internal/user`** are domains — the code that changes together.
* **`internal/postgres`** is one package, not one per domain, because a single connection pool and
  a shared set of scan helpers live there. It imports the domain packages; they never import it.
* **`internal/httpapi`** owns everything that knows about HTTP: routing, status codes,
  JSON shapes, middleware. No other package imports `net/http`.
* **`internal/config`** is imported only by `main`.
* **Tests sit beside the code they test**, in the same package, so they can reach unexported
  functions.

The shape of the dependency graph matters more than the directory names: `httpapi` → `order` →
(interfaces it declares), with `postgres` and `main` pointing inward. Nothing points back out.

## Best practices

* **Start with one package.** Split when you feel a specific pain, not preemptively.
* **Prefer domain packages over layer packages** once the service has more than one real concept.
* **Never create `utils`, `common`, `helpers`, or `models`.** Name packages for what they provide.
* **Break cycles with an interface in the consumer**, not with a shared package.
* **Wire everything in `main`**, and put the body in `run() error` so `defer` works.
* **Load config once at startup** into a struct; fail immediately if something required is missing.
* **Keep `net/http` out of every package except the HTTP one**, and SQL out of every package
  except the store.
* **Let the import graph be the review**: if you can't draw it as a DAG on a whiteboard, the
  layout is wrong regardless of how tidy the directories look.

tops out in the thousands. That difference is why Go handles "one goroutine per request" as a
normal design rather than a clever trick — and it's what

### The scheduler, briefly

Go multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads itself. Three things are involved: **G** (a goroutine),
**M** (an OS thread), and **P** (a scheduling context; there are

one per CPU core).

What's worth knowing in practice: when a goroutine blocks on a syscall — a database read, a file
write — the scheduler detaches that thread and gives the P to another goroutine, so blocking one
goroutine doesn't stall the rest. That's why ordinary blocking Go code scales without an

keyword anywhere.

A channel is a typed pipe that also **synchronizes** the goroutines using it. That second property
is the important one.

it's what applies backpressure when the producer outruns the consumer.

The slogan "share memory by communicating" is good advice that gets over-applied. When several
goroutines need to read and write one piece of shared state, a mutex is simpler, faster, and

title: Context Window
description: How Claude Code's context fills up during a session, and how to manage it.
content:
## What it is

The context window is everything Claude has "in mind" for the current session: the system prompt,
your `CLAUDE.md` and auto memory, MCP tool listings, every file it's read, every response it's
given, hook output, subagent summaries — all of it counted in tokens, all of it re-sent to the
model with every single message. This is the same context window covered generally for the model
itself in the API — what's specific to Claude Code is *what fills it automatically before you type
anything*, and what it does when it starts running out.

## What loads before you type a word

A surprising share of the window is spent before your first prompt:

* The system prompt
* Auto memory (`MEMORY.md`, capped at the first 200 lines or 25KB)
* Environment info (cwd, platform, shell, git status)
* MCP tool names (schemas stay deferred and load on demand, not upfront)
* Skill descriptions (one line each, so Claude knows what it can invoke)
* `CLAUDE.md` and unscoped `.claude/rules/*.md` files

From there, every file Claude reads, every tool result, every path-scoped rule that fires because
you touched a matching file — all of it keeps accumulating. Nothing shrinks the window
automatically except compaction.

## Checking usage

Run `/context` for a live, categorized breakdown of what's actually consuming your window right
now — including which CLAUDE.md and memory files loaded — with suggestions for trimming it. `/usage`
shows token counts and (for API-billed usage) a rough dollar cost for the session. If you want
usage visible continuously instead of on demand, the status line can be configured to show it (see
[Status Line](/docs/status-line)).

## `/compact` and auto-compact

`/compact` replaces the conversation history with a structured summary, freeing up space while
trying to keep what matters. You can steer what it keeps:

```bash
/compact focus on the auth bug fix
```

Claude Code also compacts **automatically** as the conversation approaches the model's context
limit — the same summarization pass, just triggered for you instead of by hand, so a full context
window doesn't end your session. How full it lets things get before compacting is the
**auto-compact window**, adjustable with `/autocompact 500k` (accepts a plain token count, a `k`/`M`
suffix, or a bare number treated as thousands). With nothing set, Claude Code compacts once the
conversation reaches the model's context limit.

### What survives compaction

Not everything reloads the same way after a `/compact`:

| Loaded via | After compaction |
|---|---|
| System prompt, output style | Unchanged — never part of message history |
| Project-root `CLAUDE.md`, unscoped rules | Re-injected from disk |
| Auto memory | Re-injected from disk |
| Rules with `paths:` frontmatter | Lost until a matching file is read again |
| Nested `CLAUDE.md` in subdirectories | Lost until a file in that subdirectory is read again |
| Invoked skill bodies | Re-injected, capped per skill and in total — oldest dropped first |
| Hooks | Not applicable — hooks are code, not context |

The practical consequence: an instruction you only said out loud in chat, or a path-scoped rule
that hasn't matched a file recently, can quietly disappear after a compaction. If it needs to
survive, it belongs in your project-root `CLAUDE.md`.

## `/compact` vs `/clear`

These solve different problems and it's easy to reach for the wrong one:

| | `/compact` | `/clear` |
|---|---|---|
| Keeps | A summary of the conversation | Nothing — fresh session |
| Cost to run | A real request (reads the whole conversation to summarize it) | Free |
| Use when | Continuing related work, but context is getting full | Switching to unrelated work |

**`/clear` between unrelated tasks.** Stale context from a finished task doesn't help the next one
— it just costs tokens on every subsequent message and dilutes what Claude pays attention to. Run
`/rename` first if you want to find the old session again later; `/resume` brings it back.

**`/compact` mid-task**, when you need the history but the window is filling up. Since compacting a
large context is itself an expensive request (it has to read everything it's about to summarize),
compacting *before* it's actually necessary just to "be safe" isn't free — let auto-compact do its
job unless you specifically want to steer what's kept.

## Managing context proactively

* **Delegate large reads to a subagent.** A subagent gets its own separate context window; only
  its final summary comes back to yours. Sending a big log file or a broad codebase search through
  a subagent keeps the raw content out of your main session entirely.
* **Write specific prompts.** "Add input validation to the login handler in `auth.go`" costs far
  less context than "improve this codebase," which triggers broad exploratory reads to figure out
  what you meant.
* **Keep CLAUDE.md lean.** It's loaded in full, every session, whether the current task needs it
  or not — see [Memory - CLAUDE.md](/docs/claude-md) for sizing guidance.
* **Prefer CLI tools over MCP servers where both exist.** `gh`, `aws`, `gcloud` don't add anything
  to the tool listing beyond their name; a live MCP connection can add meaningfully more, though
  full tool schemas are deferred until actually used.
* **Use hooks to pre-filter noisy output.** A `PostToolUse` hook that greps a 10,000-line test log
  down to just the failures saves the tokens of Claude reading all of it — see
  [Hooks](/docs/hooks).

## A real example

A session that's been open all afternoon debugging a flaky integration test, now switching to an
unrelated task — write a new endpoint:

```bash
# Wrong: context fills with debugging history that's now irrelevant
# to writing a new handler, and every message pays for it anyway.

/rename flaky-integration-test-debug
/clear
# fresh session — CLAUDE.md and auto memory reload, debugging history doesn't
```

Versus continuing the *same* task after a long back-and-forth that's approaching the limit:

```bash
/compact focus on what we changed in the retry logic and why the test still fails
# conversation gets summarized with that focus; you keep working on the same problem
```

Two different tools for what looks like the same symptom ("context is full, but that means one
thing before a `/clear` and another before a `/compact`").

### Adapter

### Facade

A notification system that started simple and grew — showing Strategy, Decorator, and Factory doing their jobs together.
Every piece is independently testable, retries and metrics are written once rather than three times, and adding a fourth channel touches one

## Best practices

* **Let patterns emerge.** Write the straightforward version first; refactor toward a pattern when duplication or rigidity actually shows up.
* **Prefer composition over inheritance** — Go gives you no choice, which turns out to be a feature.

title: Git Basics
description: The everyday Git commands — init, clone, add, commit, status, log, diff — and how to write good commit messages.
content:
These are the commands you'll type dozens of times a day. Get comfortable with them before moving on to branching.

## Starting a repository

`git init` creates a `.git` folder in the current directory — that folder *is* the repository. `git clone` does the same thing, but also downloads all history from a remote and points it at that remote automatically (see [Working with Remotes](/docs/git-workflow/remotes)).

## Checking status

```bash showLineNumbers
git status
```

Run this constantly. It tells you which files are untracked, modified, or staged — i.e., exactly where you are in the [three-area model](/docs/git-workflow/introduction#gits-three-area-mental-model).

## Staging changes

```bash showLineNumbers
git add file.go          # stage one file
git add file1.go file2.go # stage multiple files
git add .                 # stage everything in the current directory
git add -p                # interactively stage parts of a file (hunks)
```

## Committing

```bash showLineNumbers
git commit -m "Add rate limiting to auth endpoint"
```

A commit is a permanent snapshot of the staged changes, with a message explaining *why*. Useful flags:

```bash showLineNumbers
git commit -am "message"   # stage all tracked, modified files AND commit (skips new/untracked files)
git commit --amend         # rewrite the most recent commit (message and/or staged changes)
```

### Writing good commit messages

A widely used convention is **Conventional Commits**: `<type>: <short summary>`.

```bash showLineNumbers
git commit -m "feat: add JWT refresh token endpoint"
git commit -m "fix: prevent nil pointer on empty request body"
git commit -m "docs: update README with setup instructions"
git commit -m "refactor: extract validation logic into helper"
git commit -m "test: add table-driven tests for parser"
git commit -m "chore: bump go.mod dependencies"
```

Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`, `perf`. This convention is what makes tools like automated changelogs and semantic-version bumping possible — and it's simply easier for a human to scan `git log` when every message starts with intent.

## Viewing history

```bash showLineNumbers
git log                    # full history
git log --oneline          # one line per commit
git log --oneline --graph  # with branch/merge visualization
git log -p                 # show the actual diff for each commit
git log --author="Alice"   # filter by author
```

## Viewing changes (diff)

```bash showLineNumbers
git diff              # unstaged changes vs last commit
git diff --staged     # staged changes vs last commit
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD   # changes between two commits
```

## Best practices

* **Commit often, in small units.** A commit should represent one logical change — easy to review, easy to revert if it's wrong.
* **Write the "why," not the "what."** The diff already shows *what* changed; the message should explain *why* (context a diff can't capture).
* **Never commit secrets.** `.env` files, API keys, credentials — see [.gitignore & Git Hooks](/docs/git-workflow/gitignore-hooks) for how to prevent this before it happens.
* **Run `git status` before `git add`,** and `git diff --staged` before `git commit` — know exactly what you're about to commit.

title: Best Practices Cheatsheet
description: A condensed, one-page reference of everything in the Git Workflow section.
content:
The full reasoning behind each of these lives on the earlier pages — this page is just the condensed reference to skim when you already know the concepts and need a quick reminder.

## Commits

* Commit small, logical, single-purpose changes — not "end of day" dumps.
* Use [Conventional Commits](/docs/git-workflow/basics#writing-good-commit-messages): `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `chore:`.
* Write the *why*, not the *what* — the diff already shows what changed.
* Never commit secrets. Use `.gitignore` + environment variables (see [.gitignore & Git Hooks](/docs/git-workflow/gitignore-hooks)).
* `git diff --staged` before every `git commit` — know exactly what you're about to commit.
* Never `--amend` or rewrite a commit that's already been pushed and shared.

## Branching

* Name branches by intent: `feature/x`, `fix/x`, `chore/x` — never `test`, `wip`, `asdf`.
* Keep branches short-lived. Merge or rebase from `main` frequently to avoid painful conflicts later.
* Delete branches after merging — both locally (`git branch -d`) and on the remote.
* Default to [Feature Branch Workflow](/docs/git-workflow/workflow-strategies) unless you have a specific reason for Git Flow or Trunk-Based.

## Rebase vs Merge

* `rebase` only on branches that are **local and unshared**. Never rebase a branch others have pulled.
* `merge` is always safe, including on shared branches — it never rewrites history.
* Use `rebase -i` to clean up your own commits (squash, reword) before opening a PR.

## Remotes

* `git fetch` first if unsure what's changed remotely — it's always safe and non-destructive.
* Pull (or rebase) before you push; push is rejected if the remote has moved ahead of you.
* Never `--force` push to `main` or any shared branch. Prefer `--force-with-lease` on your own branches.

## Undoing changes

| Situation | Command |
|---|---|
| Discard uncommitted file changes | `git restore <file>` |
| Unstage a file | `git restore --staged <file>` |
| Shelve work temporarily | `git stash` |
| Undo a local, unpushed commit | `git reset --soft/--hard HEAD~1` |
| Undo a pushed/shared commit | `git revert <commit>` |

## Conflicts

1. `git status` to see conflicted files.
2. Open each file, resolve manually, delete all `<<<<<<<` / `=======` / `>>>>>>>` markers.
3. `git add <file>` for each resolved file.
4. `git commit` (merge) or `git rebase --continue` (rebase).
5. **Run your tests** before considering it done — a conflict with no markers left can still be logically wrong.
6. `git merge --abort` / `git rebase --abort` to bail out cleanly at any point.

## Pull request etiquette

* Keep PRs small and focused — easier and faster to review, easier to revert if something's wrong.
* Write a description that explains *why*, links related issues/tickets, and calls out anything reviewers should pay special attention to.
* Respond to review comments with either a fix or a clear counter-argument — don't silently ignore feedback.
* Make sure CI (tests, lint) passes before requesting review.
* Squash noisy "fix typo" / "address review" commits before merge (via `rebase -i` or the platform's "Squash and merge" button).

title: Branching & Merging
description: Isolating work in branches, and bringing it back into main with git merge.
content:
## Why branch?

A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit. Branching lets you work on a feature or fix in isolation, without touching the stable code on `main`, and without your half-finished work affecting teammates.

## Creating and switching branches

```bash showLineNumbers
git branch feature/rate-limiting     # create a branch (doesn't switch to it)
git switch feature/rate-limiting     # switch to it
# or, in one step:
git switch -c feature/rate-limiting  # create AND switch

git branch                           # list local branches
git branch -a                        # list local + remote branches
```

## The branching model

```bash showLineNumbers
git switch -c feature/rate-limiting
# ... make changes, commit ...
git add .
git commit -m "feat: add token bucket rate limiter"
```

Your branch diverges from `main` at the point you created it. You commit freely on your branch while `main` may keep moving (other people merging their own work) — Git tracks both histories independently until you merge.

## Merging

Once your feature branch is ready, merge it back into `main`:

```bash showLineNumbers
git switch main
git pull                       # make sure main is up to date first
git merge feature/rate-limiting
```

Two possible outcomes:

* **Fast-forward merge** — if `main` hasn't moved since you branched, Git just moves the `main` pointer forward. No merge commit is created.
* **Three-way merge** — if `main` *has* moved (someone else merged first), Git creates a new **merge commit** with two parents, combining both histories.

```bash showLineNumbers
git merge --no-ff feature/rate-limiting   # force a merge commit even if fast-forward is possible
```

## Deleting a branch after merge

```bash showLineNumbers
git branch -d feature/rate-limiting     # safe delete (refuses if not merged)
git branch -D feature/rate-limiting     # force delete (even if not merged)
git push origin --delete feature/rate-limiting  # delete on the remote too
```

## Best practices

* **Branch names should say what they do:** `feature/rate-limiting`, `fix/nil-pointer-auth`, `chore/upgrade-deps` — not `test`, `new-branch`, `asdf`.
* **Keep branches short-lived.** The longer a branch lives without merging, the more it diverges from `main` and the more painful the eventual merge/conflict resolution becomes.
* **Pull `main` before you branch, and again before you merge**, so you're working from the latest code.
* **Delete branches after merging.** A repo with 200 stale branches is a repo nobody trusts.

title: .gitignore & Git Hooks
description: Keeping build artifacts and secrets out of your repository, and automating checks before commits with Git hooks.
content:
## `.gitignore`

A `.gitignore` file tells Git which files/patterns to never track — build output, dependencies, local secrets, IDE settings. It lives at the repo root (nested `.gitignore` files are also allowed for folder-specific rules).

```bash showLineNumbers title=".gitignore (Go project example)"
# Binaries
/bin/
*.exe
*.test

# Dependency directories
/vendor/

# Environment / secrets
.env
.env.local
*.pem

# IDE
.vscode/
.idea/

# OS
.DS_Store
```

### Checking what's ignored

```bash showLineNumbers
git check-ignore -v path/to/file   # confirms which rule is ignoring a file (useful for debugging)
git status --ignored                # lists ignored files too
```

## Git Hooks

Hooks are scripts Git runs automatically at points in the workflow (before a commit, before a push, after a merge, etc.). They live in `.git/hooks/` as plain shell scripts, but that folder isn't committed to the repo by default — which is why most teams use a tool to manage and share hooks.

### A raw hook example

```bash showLineNumbers title=".git/hooks/pre-commit"
#!/bin/sh
# Run tests before allowing a commit
go test ./... || {
  echo "Tests failed — commit aborted."
  exit 1
}
```

Make it executable: `chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit`. Now `git commit` will run this first, and abort the commit if tests fail.

### Common hook points

| Hook | Runs when | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `pre-commit` | Before a commit is created | Lint, format, run fast tests |
| `commit-msg` | After the commit message is written | Enforce message format (e.g. Conventional Commits) |
| `pre-push` | Before `git push` | Run the full test suite, block push on failure |
| `post-merge` | After a merge completes | Auto-install dependencies if `go.mod` changed |

### Sharing hooks across a team

Because `.git/hooks/` isn't committed, teams typically use a tool like **[Husky](https://typicode.github.io/husky/)** (Node projects) or **[pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/)** (language-agnostic, popular in Go/Python projects) to define hooks in a versioned config file and install them automatically for every contributor.

```bash showLineNumbers title="pre-commit example (.pre-commit-config.yaml)"
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: go-fmt
        name: gofmt
        entry: gofmt -l -w
        language: system
        types: [go]
      - id: go-vet
        name: go vet
        entry: go vet ./...
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false
```

## Best practices

* **Add a `.gitignore` before your first commit**, not after — it's much easier than untracking files later.
* **Never rely solely on `.gitignore` for secrets.** Use environment variables and a secrets manager for anything sensitive; treat `.gitignore` as a last line of defense, not the plan.
* **Keep pre-commit hooks fast** (lint/format, not the full test suite) so they don't slow down every commit — save slower checks for `pre-push` or CI.
* **Version your hook config** (Husky/pre-commit) so every contributor gets the same checks automatically.

title: Introduction to Version Control
description: Why version control exists, and Git's core mental model — working directory, staging area, and repository.
content:
## What is version control?

Version control is a system that records changes to files over time, so you can recall specific versions later. Without it, "backup" usually means files named `final.go`, `final_v2.go`, `final_v2_ACTUALLY_FINAL.go` — which breaks down the moment more than one person touches the code.

A version control system (VCS) gives you:

* **History** — every change, who made it, and why (via commit messages).
* **Branching** — the ability to work on a new feature or fix without touching working code.
* **Collaboration** — multiple people editing the same codebase without overwriting each other.
* **Safety** — the ability to undo a bad change and recover previous states.

**Git** is a *distributed* VCS: every developer has a full copy of the repository's history on their own machine, not just a snapshot from a central server. This is why most Git operations (commit, log, diff, branch) work instantly and offline — only `push`/`pull`/`fetch` need the network.

## Git's three-area mental model

Understanding Git means understanding three areas a file passes through:

1. **Working Directory** — the actual files on disk that you edit.
2. **Staging Area (Index)** — a draft of your next commit. You choose exactly which changes go in.
3. **Repository (`.git` directory)** — the permanent, committed history.

This staging step is what makes Git different from simpler VCS tools: you don't commit "everything that changed," you commit *exactly what you `git add`ed* — which is what enables small, focused, atomic commits (more on that in [Git Basics](/docs/git-workflow/basics)).

## A file's lifecycle

Every file in a Git repository is in one of these states:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Untracked** | Git doesn't know about this file yet (new file, never `git add`ed). |
| **Unmodified / Tracked** | Committed, and unchanged since the last commit. |
| **Modified** | Tracked, and changed since the last commit — but not staged. |
| **Staged** | Modified, and marked (via `git add`) to go into the next commit. |

`git status` (covered next) tells you exactly which state every file is in — it's the single most-used command in this entire guide.

## Why this matters for you

As a first-jobber, most of the pain with Git doesn't come from not knowing commands — it comes from not knowing *which area* a change currently lives in. "I committed but my teammate doesn't see it" (it's in your local repo, not pushed). "I `git add`ed but it's not in my commit" (you edited the file again after staging it — the working directory changed again). Keeping this three-area model in your head resolves 90% of Git confusion before it starts.

title: Rebase vs Merge
description: Two different ways to combine branch histories, the trade-offs, and when to use each.
content:
Both `merge` and `rebase` integrate changes from one branch into another — but they produce very different history shapes.

## Merge: preserves history exactly as it happened

```bash showLineNumbers
git switch main
git merge feature/rate-limiting
```

Merge creates a new **merge commit** joining both branch tips. The original commits on both branches stay exactly as they were. Nothing is rewritten — which makes merge always safe, even on shared/public branches.

## Rebase: replays your commits on top of another branch

```bash showLineNumbers
git switch feature/rate-limiting
git rebase main
```

Rebase takes your branch's commits, temporarily removes them, replays `main`'s new commits, then re-applies yours **one by one on top** — as if you'd branched off the latest `main` all along. The result is a straight, linear history with no merge commit. Note the commits get **new hashes** (`D'`, `E'`) — this is a history rewrite.

## The golden rule of rebase

## Interactive rebase

`git rebase -i` lets you edit, reorder, squash, or drop commits before they land — commonly used to clean up a messy feature branch before opening a pull request.

```bash showLineNumbers
git rebase -i HEAD~3
```

This opens an editor listing your last 3 commits:

```text showLineNumbers
pick a1b2c3d feat: add rate limiter skeleton
pick e4f5g6h fix typo
pick i7j8k9l feat: add tests

# Commands:
# p, pick   = use commit as-is
# r, reword = use commit, edit the message
# s, squash = combine with previous commit, keep both messages
# f, fixup  = combine with previous commit, discard this message
# d, drop   = remove commit entirely
```

Changing `pick` to `squash`/`fixup` on the "fix typo" line folds that noisy commit into the previous one, so your PR shows 2 clean commits instead of 3 messy ones.

## Which one should you use?

| Situation | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Updating your local feature branch with the latest `main` | `rebase` (keeps history linear, easier to review) |
| Merging a finished feature branch into `main` via PR | `merge` (most teams; GitHub/GitLab "Squash and merge" is a common middle ground) |
| The branch is shared with teammates | `merge` only — never rebase it |
| Cleaning up your own messy commits before opening a PR | `rebase -i` |

title: Working with Remotes
description: Connecting to a remote repository — remote, fetch, pull, push, and tracking branches.
content:
## What is a remote?

A remote is a pointer to another copy of the repository — usually hosted on GitHub, GitLab, or similar. By convention, the remote you cloned from is named `origin`.

```bash showLineNumbers
git remote -v                                  # list remotes and their URLs
git remote add origin https://github.com/org/repo.git   # add a remote (if you started with git init)
```

## fetch vs pull

This distinction trips up a lot of beginners:

```bash showLineNumbers
git fetch origin    # download new commits/branches from the remote, but do NOT merge them
git pull origin main # fetch AND merge (or rebase, if configured) into your current branch
```

`git fetch` is always safe — it just updates your local knowledge of the remote (`origin/main`) without touching your working files. `git pull` immediately integrates those changes into your current branch, which can trigger a merge or a conflict right away.

## Pushing your work

```bash showLineNumbers
git push origin feature/rate-limiting          # push a branch for the first time
git push -u origin feature/rate-limiting        # same, but also set upstream tracking
git push                                        # once tracking is set, just this works
```

The `-u` (`--set-upstream`) flag links your local branch to a remote branch, so future `git push`/`git pull` on that branch don't need the full `origin <branch>` every time — and `git status` will tell you if you're ahead/behind the remote.

## Tracking branches

```bash showLineNumbers
git status                 # shows "Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits"
git branch -vv              # shows every local branch and what it tracks
```

## Force pushing

```bash showLineNumbers
git push --force              # dangerous: overwrites remote history
git push --force-with-lease   # safer: fails if the remote has commits you haven't seen
```

## Best practices

* **Pull before you push.** If the remote has moved, push will simply be rejected — fetch/pull (or rebase) first.
* **Push early, push often** on your own feature branches — it's a free backup and lets teammates see your work-in-progress.
* **Never force-push to `main` or any shared branch.**
* **Set up a tracking branch (`-u`)** the first time you push a new branch, so subsequent commands are simpler.

title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
description: A calm, step-by-step approach to resolving Git merge conflicts.
content:
A conflict happens when Git can't automatically decide how to combine two changes — usually because both branches edited the **same lines** of the **same file**. It is not an error and not a sign you did something wrong; it's expected in collaborative work.

## What a conflict looks like

When `git merge` or `git pull` hits a conflict, it pauses and marks the affected file(s):

```text showLineNumbers
func RateLimit(r *http.Request) bool {
<<<<<<< HEAD
    return tokenBucket.Allow(r.RemoteAddr)
=======
    return slidingWindow.Allow(r.RemoteAddr)
>>>>>>> feature/rate-limiting
}
```

* `<<<<<<< HEAD` down to `=======` — the version on **your current branch**.
* `=======` down to `>>>>>>> feature/rate-limiting` — the version from **the branch being merged in**.

## Step-by-step resolution

## Backing out entirely

If the conflict is confusing or you want to start over:

```bash showLineNumbers
git merge --abort      # cancel an in-progress merge, return to pre-merge state
git rebase --abort     # cancel an in-progress rebase, return to pre-rebase state
```

Both are completely safe — they simply undo the in-progress operation with no side effects.

## Reducing how often conflicts happen

* **Pull/rebase `main` into your branch frequently** — small, frequent conflicts are far easier to resolve than one giant conflict after a two-week-old branch finally merges.
* **Keep branches short-lived and focused** — the less two branches touch the same files, the fewer conflicts.
* **Communicate** — if you and a teammate are both about to touch the same file/function, a 30-second Slack message avoids a conflict entirely.

## Tooling tips

Most editors (VS Code, GoLand) show conflict markers with inline **"Accept Current" / "Accept Incoming" / "Accept Both"** buttons — usually faster and safer than resolving by hand in a plain text editor. `git mergetool` can also launch a configured 3-way diff tool.

</CardGrid>

title: Undoing Changes
description: reset, revert, restore, and stash — Git's four different ways to undo something, and when to use each.
content:
Git has several "undo" commands that look similar but do very different things. Picking the wrong one is how people lose work — this page is the map.

## Quick decision table

| I want to... | Command |
|---|---|
| Discard uncommitted changes to a file | `git restore <file>` |
| Unstage a file (keep the edits) | `git restore --staged <file>` |
| Temporarily shelve uncommitted work | `git stash` |
| Undo the last commit, but keep the changes | `git reset --soft HEAD~1` |
| Completely delete the last commit and its changes | `git reset --hard HEAD~1` |
| Undo a commit that's already pushed/shared | `git revert <commit>` |

## `git restore` — working directory changes

```bash showLineNumbers
git restore file.go              # discard uncommitted edits to file.go, back to last commit
git restore --staged file.go      # unstage file.go (git add undone), but keep the edits
```

## `git stash` — shelve work temporarily

Useful when you need to switch branches but aren't ready to commit:

```bash showLineNumbers
git stash                 # shelve all uncommitted changes
git stash list             # see stashed entries
git stash pop               # re-apply the most recent stash, and remove it from the stash list
git stash apply             # re-apply the most recent stash, but keep it in the list too
git stash drop               # delete a stash without applying it
```

## `git reset` — move the branch pointer

`reset` moves your current branch's pointer to a different commit. It has three modes, differing in what happens to your working directory and staging area:

```bash showLineNumbers
git reset --soft HEAD~1   # move pointer back 1 commit; keep changes staged
git reset --mixed HEAD~1  # (default) move pointer back; keep changes, but unstaged
git reset --hard HEAD~1   # move pointer back; DELETE all changes, working dir matches that commit
```

<Note title="Danger" type="danger">
  `git reset --hard` permanently discards commits AND uncommitted changes. If those commits have
  already been pushed, resetting locally does not remove them from the remote — you'd need a force
  push, which brings its own risks (see [Working with Remotes](/docs/git-workflow/remotes)).
</Note>

## `git revert` — the safe undo for shared history

Instead of removing a commit, `revert` creates a **new commit** that applies the exact opposite change:

```bash showLineNumbers
git revert a1b2c3d
```

```text showLineNumbers
Before: A - B - C (bad commit) - D
After:  A - B - C - D - C' (reverts C)
```

Because it adds to history rather than rewriting it, `revert` is always safe to use on shared branches like `main` — nobody's local history breaks.

## Which one should you actually use?

</CardGrid>

title: Git Workflow Strategies
description: Feature Branch Workflow, Git Flow, and Trunk-Based Development compared — and which to pick for a small team.
content:
Everything so far (branching, merging, rebasing) are *mechanics*. A **workflow strategy** is the *policy* a team agrees on for how those mechanics get used — when to branch, how long a branch lives, and how code reaches production.

## Feature Branch Workflow

The simplest and most common strategy: every change (feature, fix, chore) gets its own branch off `main`, and merges back via a pull request once reviewed.

* **Pros:** simple, easy to explain, works with any hosting platform's PR review flow.
* **Cons:** on its own, says nothing about *releases* — fine for a website deployed continuously, less clear for versioned software with scheduled releases.

## Git Flow

A heavier model with dedicated long-lived branches for different purposes:

* `main` — always reflects the latest **released** production code.
* `develop` — integration branch where features land before a release.
* `feature/*` — branched from `develop`, merged back into `develop`.
* `release/*` — branched from `develop` when preparing a release (final testing/bugfixes).
* `hotfix/*` — branched from `main` for urgent production fixes, merged into both `main` and `develop`.

- **Pros:** very explicit about what's released vs in-progress; good for software with scheduled, versioned releases (e.g. mobile apps, installed software).
- **Cons:** heavy process overhead for teams that deploy continuously; overkill for small teams or single-developer projects.

## Trunk-Based Development

The opposite extreme: everyone commits directly to `main` (the "trunk"), or uses very short-lived branches (hours, not weeks) that merge back constantly. Feature flags hide incomplete work in production rather than isolating it in a branch.

* **Pros:** avoids large, painful merges entirely; pairs naturally with continuous deployment and CI/CD.
* **Cons:** requires strong test coverage and CI discipline — without it, `main` breaks often.

## Comparison

| | Feature Branch | Git Flow | Trunk-Based |
|---|---|---|---|
| Branch lifetime | Days | Days–weeks | Hours |
| Best for | Most small/medium teams | Versioned releases (mobile, packaged software) | Continuous deployment, high test coverage |
| Complexity | Low | High | Low (but requires discipline/CI) |
| Release model | Deploy `main` whenever ready | Scheduled releases via `release/*` | Deploy `main` continuously |

## Recommendation for a small or solo project
