title: Tables & Data Types
description: Creating tables in PostgreSQL and choosing the right column type for each piece of data.
content:
## Creating a table

```sql showLineNumbers
CREATE TABLE users (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name       TEXT NOT NULL,
    is_active  BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
```

Each column is `name TYPE [constraints]`. Constraints (`NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `PRIMARY KEY`) are covered on the [next page](/docs/sql-postgresql-basics/constraints-keys) — this page is about the types.

## Choosing types

### Text

PostgreSQL has `TEXT`, `VARCHAR(n)`, and `CHAR(n)`. In PostgreSQL they're all the same underlying type with the same performance:

```sql showLineNumbers
name  TEXT NOT NULL,              -- use this
email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,      -- no faster, and the 255 is arbitrary
code  CHAR(10)                    -- pads with spaces. Avoid.
```

### Numbers

| Type | Use for |
|---|---|
| `INTEGER` (`int4`) | Ordinary whole numbers up to ~2.1 billion — counts, quantities |
| `BIGINT` (`int8`) | IDs, and anything that might exceed 2 billion |
| `NUMERIC(p, s)` | **Money and anything requiring exactness.** Arbitrary precision, no rounding error |
| `REAL` / `DOUBLE PRECISION` | Scientific/approximate values only |
| `BIGSERIAL` | Auto-incrementing `BIGINT` — shorthand for an identity column |

### Dates and times

```sql showLineNumbers
created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),  -- use this for events
birth_date DATE,                                 -- a calendar date, no time
duration   INTERVAL                              -- a span of time
```

### Booleans, UUIDs, and JSON

```sql showLineNumbers
is_active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
id        UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
metadata  JSONB,                    -- binary JSON: indexable, use this over JSON
tags      TEXT[]                    -- native array column
```

`JSONB` is genuinely useful for data whose shape varies, but don't reach for it as an excuse to skip schema design — you lose type checking and constraints. Structured data belongs in columns.

### Enums

Two reasonable approaches:

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Option A: TEXT with a CHECK — easy to extend, most common
status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
    CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled')),

-- Option B: a real enum type — stricter, but adding values requires ALTER TYPE
CREATE TYPE order_status AS ENUM ('pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled');
status order_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
```

`TEXT` + `CHECK` is usually the better default: changing the allowed set is a simple constraint change, and it maps to a plain `string` in Go.

## Auto-incrementing IDs

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Classic and still fine
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,

-- Modern SQL-standard equivalent (PostgreSQL 10+), slightly preferred
id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,

-- UUIDs — good when IDs must be generated by clients or be unguessable
id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
```

Sequential `BIGINT` IDs are compact and index well. UUIDs avoid coordination between services and don't leak how many records you have, at the cost of more storage and worse index locality. For a first project, `BIGSERIAL` is a perfectly good default.

## Changing tables

```sql showLineNumbers
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone TEXT;
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN phone;
ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;
ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN name SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN email TYPE VARCHAR(320);

DROP TABLE users;              -- fails if other tables reference it
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;
```

## Best practices

* **`TEXT` for strings, `TIMESTAMPTZ` for times, `NUMERIC` or integer cents for money.** These three defaults prevent most data-type regret.
* **Name tables plural and lowercase** (`users`, `orders`), columns `snake_case`. Consistency matters more than the specific choice, but this is the PostgreSQL norm — and unquoted identifiers are folded to lowercase anyway.
* **Add `created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()` to every table.** You will eventually want it, and backfilling it later is painful.
* **Prefer `NOT NULL` unless a column genuinely has an "unknown" state.** Nullable columns push complexity into every query that touches them.
* **Never change schema by hand in production** — always through a migration file that's reviewed and version-controlled.

title: Transactions
description: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and the ACID guarantees that make multi-step database changes safe.
content:
## The problem transactions solve

Consider transferring money between accounts — two updates that must both happen or neither:

```sql showLineNumbers
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
-- if the server crashes HERE, money has vanished
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
```

A transaction groups statements into a single all-or-nothing unit:

```sql showLineNumbers
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
```

Now either both updates are permanent, or — on any failure before `COMMIT` — neither ever happened.

## BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK

```sql showLineNumbers
BEGIN;                                    -- start
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, product_id) VALUES (1, 5);
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 5;
COMMIT;                                   -- make it permanent

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';
-- check the row count, and if it looks wrong:
ROLLBACK;                                 -- undo everything since BEGIN
```

Outside an explicit `BEGIN`, PostgreSQL runs every statement in its own implicit transaction — so a single statement is always atomic on its own.

## ACID

The four guarantees a transaction provides:

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Atomicity** | All statements succeed, or none do. No partial application. |
| **Consistency** | Constraints hold before and after; a transaction can't leave invalid data. |
| **Isolation** | Concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted changes. |
| **Durability** | Once committed, changes survive a crash or power loss. |

## Errors abort the whole transaction

PostgreSQL is strict here, and it surprises people coming from MySQL:

```sql showLineNumbers
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('alice@example.com', 'Alice');
INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('alice@example.com', 'Dup');  -- UNIQUE violation
SELECT * FROM users;
-- ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until
--        end of transaction block
COMMIT;   -- behaves as ROLLBACK
```

After any error, the transaction enters an aborted state and rejects everything until you `ROLLBACK`. There's no "continue past the failure" — which is the safe default.

### Savepoints

If you genuinely need to recover from one failed statement without discarding the whole transaction:

```sql showLineNumbers
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('bob@example.com', 'Bob');

SAVEPOINT sp1;
INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('bob@example.com', 'Dup');  -- fails
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;   -- undo just that, transaction stays alive

INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('carol@example.com', 'Carol');
COMMIT;   -- Bob and Carol are saved
```

Use sparingly — they add complexity, and usually `ON CONFLICT` is the better answer.

## Concurrency and locking

An `UPDATE` takes a row-level lock held until the transaction ends. Another transaction updating the same row waits.

```sql showLineNumbers
-- Session A
BEGIN;
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 5;
-- Session B's UPDATE on id = 5 now blocks here...
COMMIT;   -- ...and proceeds once A commits
```

### SELECT ... FOR UPDATE

Read-then-write is a race condition: two transactions read `stock = 1`, both decide it's fine, both decrement, stock goes to `-1`. `FOR UPDATE` locks the rows you read:

```sql showLineNumbers
BEGIN;
SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 5 FOR UPDATE;   -- locks the row
-- other transactions block here until we commit
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 5;
COMMIT;
```

<Note title="Deadlocks" type="warning">
  Two transactions each holding a lock the other wants will deadlock. PostgreSQL detects this and
  kills one with error code `40P01`. The fix is to **always acquire locks in a consistent order**
  (for example, always update the lower account id first), and to retry the aborted transaction in
  application code.
</Note>

## Keep transactions short

## Isolation levels — the short version

PostgreSQL's default is `READ COMMITTED`: each statement sees only data committed before *that statement* began. This is the right default for almost all application code.

```sql showLineNumbers
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;   -- consistent snapshot for the whole transaction
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;      -- strongest; may abort with a serialization failure
```

Stronger levels trade throughput for stricter guarantees and require retry logic. The anomalies they prevent — non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, write skew — are covered in [PostgreSQL Advanced](/docs/postgresql-advanced).

## Best practices

* **Wrap related writes in a transaction** so they can't half-apply.
* **Use `BEGIN` before manual destructive statements**, and check the row count before committing.
* **Keep transactions short** — database work only, no HTTP calls, no user input, no sleeps.
* **Always `defer tx.Rollback()`** in Go; rolling back an already-committed transaction is a harmless no-op ([details](/docs/sql-postgresql-basics/using-from-go#transactions-in-go)).
* **Prefer one atomic statement** over `SELECT` + `UPDATE` where possible.
* **Acquire locks in a consistent order** and retry on deadlock (`40P01`) or serialization failure (`40001`).

title: Status Line
description: Configuring a custom status bar in Claude Code to surface context usage, cost, and git state.
content:
## What it is

The status line is the bar at the bottom of Claude Code. By default it shows a handful of
built-in footer hints. Point the `statusLine` setting at a script, and Claude Code instead pipes
JSON session data to that script on stdin and prints whatever it writes to stdout — model name,
cost, context usage, git branch, or anything you can derive from that JSON.

It runs **locally** and costs no API tokens. Think of it as the DevOps instinct applied to your
own tooling: you wouldn't run a service without a dashboard, and a long Claude Code session is
similar — you want to see context filling up before you get compacted mid-task, and see cost
accumulating before it surprises you.

The script re-runs on session start, after each assistant message, after `/compact`, on
permission-mode changes, and on vim-mode toggles. Rapid changes are debounced to 300ms, and a
slow script gets cancelled if a new update fires while it's still running — so keep it fast.

## How to use it

### The fast path: `/statusline`

```text
/statusline show model name and context percentage with a progress bar
```

Claude Code writes a script to `~/.claude/` and wires up `settings.json` for you. This is the
right default — read the next section to understand what it generated, then hand-edit from there.

### Manual configuration

Add a `statusLine` block to `~/.claude/settings.json` (or a project's `.claude/settings.json`):

```json title="settings.json"
{
  "statusLine": {
    "type": "command",
    "command": "~/.claude/statusline.sh",
    "padding": 2
  }
}
```

`command` runs in a shell, so a script path or an inline one-liner both work:

```json title="settings.json"
}
```



Claude Code sends one JSON object per invocation. The fields that matter for a backend/DevOps
workflow:

| Field | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `model.display_name`, `model.id` | Which model is running |
| `cwd`, `workspace.current_dir` | Current working directory |
| `workspace.project_dir` | Where the session was launched, if you've `cd`'d since |
| `workspace.repo.host/owner/name` | Parsed from the `origin` remote |
| `cost.total_cost_usd` | Estimated session cost, resets on `/clear` |
| `cost.total_duration_ms`, `cost.total_api_duration_ms` | Wall-clock vs. time waiting on the API |
| `cost.total_lines_added`, `cost.total_lines_removed` | Diff size for the session so far |
| `context_window.used_percentage`, `.remaining_percentage` | Pre-calculated, input-tokens-only |
| `context_window.context_window_size` | 200k by default, 1M for extended-context models |
| `rate_limits.five_hour.used_percentage`, `.seven_day.used_percentage` | Pro/Max subscription limits, absent for API-key usage |
| `session_id` | Stable per session — useful as a cache key, not a PID |
| `pr.number`, `pr.url`, `pr.review_state` | Open PR for the current branch, if any |
| `vim.mode` | Only present when vim mode is on |

`git branch --show-current` and `git diff --numstat` from inside the script, same as you would.

`used_percentage` is computed from input tokens only (\`input\_tokens + cache\_creation\_input\_tokens

* cache\_read\_input\_tokens`); it does not include output tokens. If you compute context percentage

  what Claude Code shows elsewhere.

* **Cache anything that shells out.** `git status` and `git diff` are cheap once, expensive when
  a script re-running on every message calls them dozens of times a minute. Key the cache file
  off `session_id` — not `$$` or a PID, which change on every invocation and defeat the point.
* **Handle absence, not just null.** `workspace.repo`, `pr`, `rate_limits`, and `vim` are entirely
  *absent* from the JSON outside a git repo, outside an open PR, on API-key billing, or with vim
  mode off — `jq`'s `// empty` (not `// 0`) is the idiom for "print nothing if this isn't there."

  notifications, which can truncate a long line on a narrow terminal.
* **Set `refreshInterval` only for time-based data.** Event-driven updates cover model changes,
  new messages, and compaction; add a timer only if you're rendering a clock or you have
  background subagents that might change git state while the main session sits idle.
* **Test with a fixture, not by guessing.** Pipe a minimal JSON blob straight into the script
  before wiring it into settings — this catches `jq` typos before they show up as a blank bar.

```bash showLineNumbers title="~/.claude/statusline.sh"
DIR=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.workspace.current_dir')

if [ "$PCT" -ge 90 ]; then BAR_COLOR="$RED"
elif [ "$PCT" -ge 70 ]; then BAR_COLOR="$YELLOW"
else BAR_COLOR="$GREEN"; fi
```

title: Subagents
description: Delegating work to an isolated context window with its own system prompt, tools, and model.
content:
## What it is

A subagent is a specialized assistant that runs a task in **its own context window**, with its
own system prompt, its own tool access, and its own permissions — separate from your main
conversation. When Claude spots a task matching a subagent's `description`, it delegates: the
subagent works independently and returns a summary, while everything it read or ran along the way
stays out of your main context.

This solves a specific problem: exploring a codebase, running a test suite, or grepping through
logs can produce thousands of lines you'll never look at directly and don't want permanently
occupying your context window. A subagent absorbs that noise and hands back only the finding.

Claude Code ships three built-in subagents you'll see used automatically: **Explore** (read-only,
codebase search), **Plan** (read-only research used during plan mode), and **general-purpose**
(full tool access, for tasks that need both exploration and edits). You define your own for
anything you keep delegating the same way, with the same instructions, across sessions.

## How to use it

### Write one

Subagents are markdown files with YAML frontmatter, stored in `.claude/agents/` (project-scoped)
or `~/.claude/agents/` (personal, every project). The fastest way to get a well-formed one is to
describe it and let Claude write the file:

```text
Create a personal code-improver subagent in ~/.claude/agents/ that scans
files and suggests improvements for readability, performance, and best
practices. Make it read-only and have it use Sonnet.
```

Which produces something like:

```markdown title="~/.claude/agents/code-improver.md"
---
name: code-improver
description: Scans files and suggests improvements for readability, performance, and best practices. Use after writing or modifying code.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
model: sonnet
---

You are a code improvement specialist. For each issue you find, explain
the problem, show the current code, and provide an improved version.
```

The body is the subagent's **entire** system prompt — a subagent doesn't inherit Claude Code's
default system prompt, only this file plus basic environment info like the working directory.

### Frontmatter fields

Only `name` and `description` are required.

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `name` | Unique identifier (lowercase, hyphens). No colons — those are reserved for plugin-scoped names like `my-plugin:reviewer`. |
| `description` | What the subagent is for — this is what Claude matches against a task to decide whether to delegate. |
| `tools` | Allowlist of tools the subagent may use. Omit to inherit everything available to subagents. |
| `disallowedTools` | Denylist, applied *before* `tools` is resolved against what remains. |
| `model` | `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `fable`, a full model ID, or `inherit` (default). Route cheap, well-scoped work to a smaller model here. |
| `permissionMode` | `default`, `acceptEdits`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions`, or `plan`. |
| `skills` | Skills whose **full content** preloads into the subagent's context at startup — see [Agent Skills](/docs/agent-skills). |
| `mcpServers` | MCP servers scoped to just this subagent, connected on start and torn down on finish. |
| `maxTurns` | Hard cap on agentic turns before the subagent stops. |
| `isolation: worktree` | Runs the subagent against a temporary git worktree instead of your working copy. |
| `memory` | `user`, `project`, or `local` — gives the subagent a persistent directory it can read/write across sessions. |

### How delegation happens

Three escalating ways to trigger a subagent, from a suggestion Claude can ignore to a session-wide
default:

1. **Natural language** — name it in your prompt (`"use the test-runner subagent to fix failing
   tests"`); Claude decides whether to actually delegate.
2. **@-mention** — `@code-reviewer look at the auth changes` guarantees that specific subagent
   runs for this task rather than leaving the choice to Claude.
3. **Session-wide** — `claude --agent code-reviewer` (or an `"agent"` key in
   `.claude/settings.json`) makes the subagent's system prompt, tools, and model the main
   session's defaults for the whole session.

A subagent inherits the tools available to subagents generally, narrowed by whatever `tools` /
`disallowedTools` you set, and further narrowed if it runs in the background (the default as of
recent versions) — background subagents keep a smaller built-in tool set than foreground ones,
though every permission prompt they hit still surfaces in your main session for you to approve or
deny.

## Best practices

* **Write a specific `description`.** It's the only thing Claude matches against when deciding
  whether to delegate automatically — vague descriptions mean vague (or absent) delegation. Add
  "use proactively" if you want Claude to reach for it without being asked.
* **Restrict `tools` to what the task actually needs.** A subagent that only searches code should
  not have `Write` or `Edit` — this is the same instinct as least-privilege IAM policies, applied
  to an agent instead of a service account.
* **Route to a cheaper model when the task doesn't need your main model's reasoning.** Log
  triage, mechanical greps, and rote summarization are good candidates for `model: haiku`.
* **Check subagent definitions into version control** when they're project-specific — a
  teammate's session should get the same restricted, well-scoped researcher you built, not have
  to reconstruct it from memory.
* **Don't run everything through a subagent.** A quick file read or a two-line edit belongs in
  the main conversation; delegating it just adds round-trip overhead for no isolation benefit.
  Reach for a subagent when the *volume* of intermediate output — not the importance of the task
  — is what you're trying to keep out of your main context.

### Subagents vs. skills vs. plain instructions

The deciding question is **volume of intermediate output**, not complexity. A skill's content
loads into your *existing* context and stays there. A subagent gets an entirely separate context
window and returns only a summary — that's the isolation a big `grep` sweep or a full test-suite
run actually needs. A one-off instruction that won't recur isn't worth formalizing as either.

They compose rather than substitute for each other: a skill with `context: fork` runs its
instructions inside a subagent for isolation, and a subagent's `skills:` field preloads skill
content as reference material for that subagent's system prompt. See
[Agent Skills](/docs/agent-skills#skills-vs-slash-commands-subagents-and-mcp) for the full
comparison table including MCP.

## A real example

A read-only database subagent, scoped so it can query but never mutate — a `PreToolUse` hook
enforces the boundary at the command level rather than relying on the system prompt alone:

```markdown title=".claude/agents/db-reader.md"
---
name: db-reader
description: Execute read-only database queries for debugging and investigation. Use when the user needs to check data without modifying it.
tools: Bash
model: haiku
hooks:
  PreToolUse:
    - matcher: "Bash"
      hooks:
        - type: command
          command: "./scripts/validate-readonly-query.sh"
---

You investigate data issues by running read-only SQL queries. Explain what you're
querying and why before running it. Never attempt a write — if the task requires
one, say so and stop.
```

```bash showLineNumbers title="scripts/validate-readonly-query.sh"
#!/bin/bash
INPUT=$(cat)
COMMAND=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty')

if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -iE '\b(INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|CREATE|ALTER|TRUNCATE)\b' > /dev/null; then
  echo "Blocked: Only SELECT queries are allowed" >&2
  exit 2
fi

exit 0
```

Two layers of restriction here: `tools: Bash` (nothing else, so it can't reach for `Write`) plus
a hook that inspects every Bash command before it runs. The system prompt asks nicely; the hook
is what actually enforces it — the same layered-trust habit from [evaluating third-party
skills](/docs/skills-ecosystem), applied to something you wrote yourself.

title: tmux - Terminal Multiplexer
description: Persistent, multi-pane terminal sessions that survive SSH disconnects.
content:
## What it is

`tmux` (terminal multiplexer) runs your shell sessions inside a background server process
instead of inside your terminal window. The terminal you're looking at is just a client attached
to that server. Close the terminal, lose the SSH connection, put your laptop to sleep — the
session keeps running, and you reattach to exactly where you left it.

That single property solves a problem every backend/DevOps engineer hits early: a long-running
job (a migration, a build, `tail -f` on a production log) dies the moment the connection that
started it drops. Without tmux, `nohup` and `&` are the workaround. With tmux, you just don't
think about it — you SSH back in and `tmux attach`.

The second thing tmux buys you is **panes and windows** — splitting one terminal into several,
each running its own shell, without opening new terminal emulator windows or new SSH connections.

## Core concepts

tmux has a three-level hierarchy. Get this straight and every command reads as "do X to the thing
at level Y":

* **Server** — one background process per machine, started automatically by the first `tmux`
  command. You rarely interact with it directly.
* **Session** — a named workspace, typically one per project or task (`deploy`, `monitoring`).
  Detaching leaves it running; attaching reconnects to it. This is the unit that survives
  disconnects.
* **Window** — a full-screen tab within a session, like a browser tab. Each window has its own
  name and can hold one or many panes.
* **Pane** — a subdivision of a window, each running an independent shell. Splitting panes is how
  you watch several things at once without extra windows or connections.

Every session, window, and pane has an index or name, and every tmux command targets one of them
with a **target syntax**: `session:window.pane` (e.g. `deploy:1.0`). Most day-to-day usage never
types this — you navigate with keybindings instead — but it's what `-t` flags take when you script
tmux.

## How to use it

Every tmux command is either typed at a shell prompt (`tmux new -s name`) or sent as a
**keybinding after a prefix key**. The default prefix is `Ctrl-b`: press it, release it, then
press the command key. `Ctrl-b %` means "press Ctrl-b, let go, then press `%`" — not all three at
once.

### Sessions

```bash
tmux new -s deploy          # create and attach a new session named "deploy"
tmux ls                     # list all sessions on this server
tmux attach -t deploy       # attach to an existing session (tmux a -t deploy also works)
tmux kill-session -t deploy # kill a session and everything in it
```

| Keybinding | Action |
|---|---|
| `prefix d` | Detach from the current session (it keeps running) |
| `prefix $` | Rename the current session |
| `prefix s` | Interactive session picker |

### Windows

| Keybinding | Action |
|---|---|
| `prefix c` | Create a new window |
| `prefix ,` | Rename the current window |
| `prefix n` / `prefix p` | Next / previous window |
| `prefix 0`–`9` | Jump to window by number |
| `prefix w` | Interactive window picker |
| `prefix &` | Kill the current window (asks for confirmation) |

### Panes

| Keybinding | Action |
|---|---|
| `prefix %` | Split pane vertically — new pane to the **right** |
| `prefix "` | Split pane horizontally — new pane **below** |
| `prefix` arrow key | Move focus to the pane in that direction |
| `prefix o` | Cycle focus to the next pane |
| `prefix q` | Briefly show pane numbers (then press a number to jump) |
| `prefix z` | Zoom the current pane to fullscreen (toggle) |
| `prefix x` | Kill the current pane (asks for confirmation) |
| `prefix Ctrl-arrow` | Resize the current pane |

### Copy mode

Your mouse scroll wheel won't scroll tmux's buffer by default. Enter copy mode with `prefix [`,
navigate with arrow keys or vi bindings (`j`/`k`), and press `q` to exit. With `set -g mouse on`
in your config (below), the mouse wheel and click-to-select-pane work as expected, which is the
first thing most people turn on.

## A starter `~/.tmux.conf`

tmux reads `~/.tmux.conf` on startup (or on `prefix :` then `source-file ~/.tmux.conf` to reload
without restarting). This is a reasonable starting point — comment out anything you don't want:

```bash showLineNumbers title="~/.tmux.conf"
# Remap prefix from Ctrl-b to Ctrl-a — closer to the home row, and matches screen.
unbind C-b
set -g prefix C-a
bind C-a send-prefix

# Mouse support: click to select panes, scroll to scroll, drag to resize.
set -g mouse on

# Start window and pane numbering at 1, not 0 — matches the keyboard row.
set -g base-index 1
setw -g pane-base-index 1

# Renumber windows automatically when one is closed.
set -g renumber-windows on

# Scrollback buffer size (default is only 2000 lines).
set -g history-limit 50000

# Faster key repetition — default escape delay hurts vim/nvim inside tmux.
set -sg escape-time 0

# More intuitive split keybindings, opened in the current pane's directory.
bind | split-window -h -c "#{pane_current_path}"
bind - split-window -v -c "#{pane_current_path}"
bind c new-window -c "#{pane_current_path}"

# Reload config without restarting the server.
bind r source-file ~/.tmux.conf \; display "Config reloaded"

# Status bar: session name left, host + time right.
set -g status-style bg=black,fg=white
set -g status-left "#[bold]#S "
set -g status-right "%H:%M  #h"

# Correct terminal type for full color support in vim/nvim and other TUIs.
set -g default-terminal "tmux-256color"
```

## Best practices

* **Name sessions for what they're for**, not for the date or a number — `deploy`, `db-migrate`,
  `incident-2024-08` are all things you'll recognize a week later; `1` and `2` are not.
* **One session per task or project**, not one giant session with forty windows. `tmux ls` should
  read like a table of contents.
* **Start long or risky jobs inside tmux by default** on any remote box — migrations, deploys,
  data backfills. Losing the SSH connection five minutes into a two-hour job is a bad way to learn
  this lesson.
* **Detach, don't close the terminal.** `prefix d` leaves the session running; closing the
  terminal window (or losing the connection) also leaves it running, but detaching is the
  intentional version and doesn't risk killing a foreground process with `Ctrl-C` on the way out.
* **Kill sessions you're done with.** `tmux ls` accumulates forgotten sessions fast, each one a
  live shell (and possibly a live process) nobody's watching.
* **Turn mouse mode on early** if you're new to tmux — it removes the biggest friction (scrolling,
  pane selection) while you build keybinding muscle memory, and doesn't stop you from using the
  keyboard shortcuts alongside it.

## A real example

SSH into a server to run a migration and keep an eye on logs at the same time, in a way that
survives your laptop going to sleep:

```bash
ssh deploy@db-primary
tmux new -s migrate          # start a named session
```

Split the window so the migration and the log tail run side by side:

```
prefix %                      # split vertically → two panes, side by side
```

In the left pane:

```bash
make migrate-up
```

In the right pane (`prefix →` or `prefix o` to switch focus):

```bash
tail -f /var/log/app/migration.log
```

Now detach with `prefix d` and close the laptop. Later, from anywhere:

```bash
ssh deploy@db-primary
tmux attach -t migrate        # back exactly where you left it, migration still running
```

If the migration finished while you were away, the log tail shows the whole history because it's
still in the pane's scrollback — nothing was lost by not watching it live.
